activities.title: Oral Language Development: Community Circle Time
activities.content:
Greeting / Kuuñinde
• Welcome pupils and have them sit in a circle. 
• Say: Xaranllenmu bisimilla an na i  taxundi xo komponoone. 
• Say: O da a joppa ti kuuñinden ⴄa. O na me kuuñi ti o kittiteyen ⴄa. O su na o kittiteyen 
wutu kammun di.. 
• Check to make sure every pupil is holding up the right hand.
• Say:  An ga na sere kuuñi, an na i giyan koorosi siri, an na a toxon ko, an na kuuñi.
• Turn to the pupil on your right, shake their hand.
• Say: (say the student's name). Xa wuyi jam di, (an na xaranllenmu ku toxonun ko). 
• Pupil should respond back saying "Good morning, teacher."
• Have the pupil that was just greeted, turn to the pupil on their right and greet them. 
This  continues all the way around the circle.
Theme Discussion
· Say: (Haten suuhunu) Xaranñime (A su na do inke ya yi- Haten sufunu)
• Before school starts, bring in two items related to the theme to show the pupils. Put the   
items in the center of the circle. If no items are available, draw two pictures on the board  
 instead.
• Say: Ke koye di, o xaranñimmen ñaana ''haten suuhunu'' xaranⴄen ya yi.
• Hold up one of the items from the center of the circle. 

• Say: Mani ni ke yi?
• Call on a pupil at random to answer.
• Say: Xa rawayi mani koninin n da ke moxo di?
• Call on 2-3 pupils at random to answer. Repeat with the second item.
• Say: O gaa ke be di a do 'xaranñimme' ke da me wari kan moxo di?
• Give pupils one minute to think, even close their eyes to picture their response. Then 
choose one of the following options for discussion: call on pupils at random, Turn and Talk 
(have pupils turn to a pupil next to them), go around the circle and allow every pupil to 
answer (only if the answer is short), or have pupils take turns acting out answers.
• Encourage pupils to bring in their own items relating to the theme throughout the week.

activities.title: Letter of the Week
activities.content:
Learning Letter "a" "A"
• Write the small letter "a" very big on the board. Point to the letter.
• Say: O wa riini suugu hibe ga o demana nan katu sigiru ku saxu moxon xarana honne 
honne. Ke wa o deemana na sigiru xottun xara.
• Point to the letter on the board or letter card, say the sound, have pupils repeat 3 times   
slowly.
• Write the capital letter "A" very big on the board. Point to the capital letter.
• Say.  Ke ni xotti banne ya yi. A sehexanne ni /a/. O na a walla digantan jopperan ⴄa, seren 
toxo ma digiran toxo.
• Point to the letter on the board or letter card, say the sound, have pupils repeat 3 times  
slowly.
• Point to the small letter "a" on the board or letter card again.
• Say: A gaban gabe, o wa a walla diganqannun noxon di.

activities.title: Writing
activities.content:
Fine Motor Development
• Say: O su na o kittun bogu me di, ken na o deemana o ga katunu sahandini moxo be.
•  The stronger the muscles in our hands, the better we can control our hands when writing.
• Exercise is marching: standing in place the opposite arm swings forward to the raised 
knee (left arm and right knee together). As pupils march on the spot, give orders: low 
march knees raised slightly), normal march (knees raised to half raised), high march 
(knees raised as high as possible), left turn, right turn, face forward.
• Alternative exercise is the crab walk: (make sure the ground is not dirty so pupils do 
not soil their clothes) sit on the ground with legs extended out in front, place hands by 
side with fingers pointed toward feet, lift body up into the air, start moving forward or 
backwards. Have pupils try for one minute then have them stop and rest for a minute.    
 Then have them try again for another minute.

lessons.homework: Ask learners to teach their family members the letter name and sound they learnt today.

Annex I:  Techniques for Teaching
 
 
 
Gambia Rise Foundational Learning Lessons 
I do | We do | You do 
This is a process to slowly shift from the teacher demonstrating a new skill or concept, to the pupil 
doing it on their own.
• I DO: The teacher models or demonstrates, and explains what they are doing.
• WE DO: The teacher and pupils practice the skill or task together, once or several times
• YOU DO: Pupils try it alone, with many opportunities to practice with the same and new   
  material 
 
Turn and Talk 
Using this technique, a teacher would give pupils a task, then ask them to turn and talk to another 
pupil sitting next to them. Usually, pupils must do this quickly, then turn back to the teacher. Using 
this teaching technique, teachers can get all the pupils in the class to actively think about and discuss 
the response to a question, or practice a skill. For example, if asking a comprehension question, the 
teacher has all pupils turn and talk quickly with the person next to them about their response to the 
question. By doing this, all the pupils are expected to pay attention, to think about what is being 
asked, and to be ready with a response.  Also, it provides a way to do continuous assessment - to 
assess, just walk around and listen to what the pupils are saying or doing. Finally, pupils who don't 
speak the Ghanaian Language of Instruction can use this time to think and talk in their language, 
before giving a response in the Language of Instruction.  Note: You must be ready to let your room 
get a little noisy, and be sure to have a consistent signal for pupils to start and stop the Turn and Talk 
activity so you can use it quickly and then move on with the lesson.   
 
Calling on pupils "at random" 
Calling on pupils at random, instead of calling on pupils to volunteer, accomplishes two things. First, 
it helps pupils understand that they should always be ready to share their thoughts. They should be 
actively listening to the teacher all the time, and thinking about the activities and discussions. 
Second, it gives the teacher insight into what pupils are understanding and why they may not be 
interested in responding. By including both the brightest pupils and pupils who need more explanation 
or demonstration to understand the lesson, helps the teacher reach all pupils.   
 
Whole class response 
Activities that call for the whole class to respond in unison are a way for the teacher to monitor who 
has understood, and who has not understood. It helps the teacher know which pupils need more 
support and gives the teacher a chance to pause the lesson and give feedback to individuals or groups 
of pupils who are not following along. For whole class response to be effective, pupils must respond 
all together, immediately. For example, if they are to put up two fingers to say "yes" and one to say 
"no," then they must do this as soon as the teacher signals (gives them a cue) for them to respond. 
Note that pupils may need a bit of time to think before responding, so the teacher may wait before 
giving the signal. But if some pupils are permitted to respond before others, the slower pupils may 
simply copy the classmates who respond first. So be sure to give them a signal, and encourage them 
to respond right away! 
 

Annex lI:    Techniques  to Support Second Languager Learners 
 
 
Create links to personal experience and background knowledge 
 
Why? L2 learners benefit from understanding the context of new materials. Relating the new 
material to their experiences and background knowledge provides meaningful context. 
How? When introducing a topic, ask pupils what they know about it. Have they ever seen, used, or 
done this thing? When? Turn and talk works well for this type of strategy. Pupils can first think about 
what they already know, then turn to a partner to talk about it. After that, a few pupils can share 
with the whole class.  
 
Encourage pupils to use their home language (L1)  
 
Why? Using the more familiar language (L1) to learn a less familiar language (L2) can help pupils 
clarify their understandings of classroom conversation and text, confirm and expand their 
understanding of the content, prepare to carry out a task in the L2, and talk about how their 
language works. It can also save time by allowing for the occasional quick translation, rather than 
undergoing a long attempt at explanation in the L2. Additionally, it can give pupils a sense of security 
when much of what is happening in the classroom is new.  
 
How? Using L1 in the classroom needs to be done carefully with intentional planning. Regular code 
switching (changing back and forth) from L2 to L1 without a planned strategy may result in linguistic 
confusion. To avoid confusion and save time when explaining new vocabulary, systematically ask 
pupils as part of the instructional routine, "How would you say this in your language?" Likewise, after 
reading a story, ask pupils to retell the story in their own language. A rule of thumb for deciding on 
the use of L1 is to consider if the pupils' understanding of the content is important or how to express 
a message in the L2. For example, when pupils share their prior experience with a new word or 
concept, using L1 can be helpful because what is important is to connect to their experiences, not 
how to express that in the L2. Similarly, when pupils are preparing a partner or group task, they may 
be invited to use the L1 but reminded that the ultimate product (such as a verbal or written response) 
should be in the L2. This encourages deeper thinking about the topic and allows for discussion in the 
L1 about the L2 as pupils prepare their work. 
 
Practice and play with the sounds of the target language  
Why? After vocabulary, phonological awareness is one of the most important skills for L2 readers to 
develop. Even if sounds are similar in the L1 and L2, pupils who are new to the L2 will need to develop 
their capacity to hear those same sounds in a new linguistic context. The first skills to develop are 
more general phonological awareness skills, such as identifying individual words in a spoken sentence 
and identifying rhyme. Finer skills such as identifying syllables and phonemes (individual sounds) and 
being able to substitute or delete syllables or phonemes are developed later.  
How? Teachers can make a habit of integrating some phonological awareness whenever they are 
introducing new words and phrases, and returning to phonological awareness work if pupils are 
struggling to read certain passages or spell certain words. Techniques include representing spoken 
words with pebbles or bottle caps, clapping the syllables in a new vocabulary word, and finding words 
pupils already know that rhyme or contain a similar sound to a new word..  
 
Enhance meaning with pictures, objects, and actions 
Why? L2 learners need to interact with a new word or idea many times and in many ways to fully 

learn the meaning. Using pictures, objects, and actions can help provide visual, tactile, and 
kinesthetic reinforcement to any verbal explanation that may be given for a new word. 
How? It does not matter if you do not have fancy, prepared flash cards and posters. Teachers can 
draw simple stick figures and line drawings on the board (or ask pupils to do it). The teacher and the 
pupils can use actions to demonstrate individual words and concepts, or can use role play to 
dramatize stories they have read. Many everyday objects are portable enough for teachers to bring 
to school to use for demonstrations (e.g., dishes, clothing, cooking tools, parts of plants, etc.). Keep 
clippings of images from newspapers and magazines as small treasures to share and discuss on the 
right occasion. Parents' committees can also help collect empty containers that can be used in class 
for demonstration and vocabulary practice (e.g., old containers for different foods and drinks, empty 
medicine packets, labels of various products, etc.). 
 
Give pupils time to process and test out ideas, either by speaking in their first or in their new 
language, with a partner or small group   
 
Why? In an L2 classroom, it is important to have learners feel secure so that they can take risks and 
participate fully. They will feel more secure if they have time to practice using their L2 and answering 
the question before having to say it in front of the whole class. While this cannot be used for every 
question in every class, it is important to remember to do this several times each lesson so that the 
pupils who tend to take longer to prepare an answer and who do not frequently raise their hands 
have more opportunity to participate in a non-threatening way. 
 
How? Pupils may be asked to jot down their idea on a slate or in their notebooks, or to think quietly 
and then participate in a turn and talk. Another way to encourage participation from even the 
quietest pupils is to ask a whole-class question that has two or more possible answers and all pupils 
answer at once. For example, a teacher might say, "In the story today, would you describe the main 
character as brave or foolish? Raise your fist if you think she was brave and raise one finger if you 
think she was foolish."
